title: Low blood pressure and raised pressures on a fast rate
summary: A 58-year-old ventilated man with a high rate on volume control has raised pressures and low blood pressure.
rationale: A long inspiratory time (slow flow) at a fast rate leaves too little time to exhale: gas is trapped (auto-PEEP), Pplat and Ppk rise together and venous return falls. A slower rate with faster flow restores the expiratory time. Headless engine check on the starting settings and after the named actions: untouched by 2 min: PaCO2 28, pH 7.55, SpO2 93%, Pplat 26, auto-PEEP 5.3, SBP 88; untouched by 30 min: PaCO2 26, pH 7.57, SpO2 93%, Pplat 26, auto-PEEP 5.3, SBP 88; reasonable management by 30 min: PaCO2 36, pH 7.47, SpO2 94%, Pplat 21, SBP 108; typical mistake by 30 min: PaCO2 26, pH 7.57, SpO2 92%, Pplat 28, auto-PEEP 7.3, SBP 82. Values for an arm whose case ended early (improved or deteriorated trigger) are the values when it ended.

retestsMistake.clinicalFocus: Breath stacking: a high rate and slow inspiratory flow leave too little expiratory time; lower the rate and raise the flow before looking for other causes

source: The Ventilator Book 3e (alarms / troubleshooting and respiratory mechanics chapters, numbers unverified); Marino ICU Book 2025 (ventilator-associated complications and airway pressure chapters, unverified); Nunn & Lumb 9e (resistance and compliance chapters, unverified); Hess DR. Respir Care 2014;59:1773-94 (peak minus plateau pressure); Marino ICU Book 2025 (auto-PEEP chapter, number unverified). Expiratory resistance 28 and RR 24 are teaching assumptions (unverified).

changes.vignette: Male 58, 172 cm, 75 kg. VC 560 mL, RR 24, flow 30 L/min, PEEP 5, FiO2 0.4.

patient.presentingStory: Ventilated after an aspiration. The rate was raised to 24 per minute overnight for a rising CO2 and the flow was dropped to 30 L/min because he looked uncomfortable. The pressure alarm is now sounding and the blood pressure is lower.
patient.history: Aspiration pneumonia, mild chronic bronchitis. Full escalation.

findings.examine: Sedated. Equal air entry, prolonged expiration with the expiratory flow still positive at the next breath. Neck veins flat. Tube at 22 cm at the teeth.
findings.cxr: Tube 4 cm above the carina, right lower zone consolidation, mild hyperinflation, no pneumothorax.

evidence.claim: Trapped gas from insufficient expiratory time raises both peak and plateau pressures and lowers venous return.
evidence.source: Marino PL. Marino's The ICU Book, 2025 edition (chapter on ventilator troubleshooting; number unverified)

evidence.claim: Measurement of plateau pressure via inspiratory hold differentiates high resistance (elevated Ppeak, normal Pplat) from low compliance (both Ppeak and Pplat elevated).
evidence.source: Hess DR. Respiratory mechanics in the mechanically ventilated patient. Respir Care 2014;59(11):1773-1794

actions.text: The suction catheter passes freely to the carina and returns scant clear secretions. The pressures are unchanged.
Salbutamol given through the circuit. There is no obvious change in the airway pressures.
The senior says: what do the peak and plateau pressures show, and where does the tube sit? Work through the DOPE checklist.
Furosemide 40 mg given and the urine output rises a little. There is no immediate change in the airway pressures.

then.reason: The cause of the high airway pressure was found and treated; pressures, blood pressure and oxygenation have recovered.
The high airway pressure was not corrected, and the patient became profoundly hypotensive or hypoxaemic.

then.detail: A high peak airway pressure persisted for 7 minutes without a structured check (DOPE: tube, obstruction, pneumothorax, equipment) and an inspiratory hold to separate resistance from compliance.

rubric.description: Examined the patient within 8 minutes of the alarm
Brought peak pressure to 32 cmH2O or below
Checked a blood gas within 20 minutes

keyPoints: High pressures plus falling blood pressure on a fast rate with incomplete expiration suggest auto-PEEP; look at the expiratory flow returning to zero before the next breath.
A brief disconnection or an expiratory hold confirms it; the fix is a lower rate, faster inspiratory flow (shorter Ti) and treating the airway obstruction.
Adding more PEEP in a patient with this problem can worsen hyperinflation unless there is flow limitation.
